history.heading: Celts and Vikings
paragraphs: The Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland. It was home to Celtic people who spoke a Gaelic language, and Christianity arrived early. Norse Vikings settled from the 9th century, and the island became the centre of the Kingdom of Mann and the Isles.
The Norse established Tynwald, the island's parliament, which claims to be the oldest continuous parliament in the world, dating from 979.

history.heading: Scottish and English rule
paragraphs: Scotland took the island in 1266, and England gained control in the 14th century. From 1405 it was ruled by the Stanley family, Earls of Derby, as Lords of Mann. The British Crown purchased the lordship in 1765. The island became popular for tourism in the Victorian era.

culture.heading: Manx identity
paragraphs: English is spoken by all, while the Manx Gaelic language, whose last native speaker died in 1974, has been revived and is taught in schools. The three-legged triskelion is the island's symbol, and Manx cats, which have no tail, are famous.

The TT (Tourist Trophy) motorcycle races, held on public roads since 1907, are among the most famous and dangerous in the world. Tynwald Day, 5 July, features an open-air ceremony where new laws are proclaimed.

politics.heading: Crown Dependency
paragraphs: The Isle of Man is a self-governing British Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom or the EU. The British monarch holds the title Lord of Mann. Tynwald makes laws, and a chief minister leads the government. The UK is responsible for defence and international relations.

economy.heading: Finance and e-gaming
paragraphs: The economy has shifted from fishing, farming and tourism to financial services, insurance, online gambling, digital businesses, and ship and aircraft registration, supported by low taxes. The Manx pound is at par with the British pound.
